interactions.summary: Jiang explains the medieval Catholic constraint he thinks the scene assumes: suicide is treated as a worse sin than rape because bodily violation does not touch the soul, which belongs to God. He then asks again why Piccarda still remains in the lower sphere if bodily coercion does not matter.

Students try to solve the bind by suggesting that the body is still God's gift and that true free will might require fighting back, even unto death. One student asks whether Dante is making an exception for suicide, and Jiang rejects that outright while insisting the deeper paradox remains.

speaker_notes.note: This packet contains Jiang's forceful classroom characterization of medieval Catholic teaching and Augustine's argument, not a neutral historical summary. Keep it framed as his interpretive explanation of the scene's constraints.

claims.claim: Jiang says that within the Catholic framework relevant to Dante, suicide is treated as the worst sin, worse than being raped, because self-killing destroys what should remain oriented toward God.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture characterization given on 2026-06-17 about Dante's religious context.

claims.claim: Jiang invokes Augustine to argue that bodily violation does not touch the soul, so what matters is the soul's relation to God rather than what happens to the body on earth.
Jiang uses that body-soul distinction to restate the paradox: if marriage or rape cannot injure the soul, why is Piccarda still ranked in the lower sphere?
A student suggests the body may still count as something God gave, so refusing or enduring torture might be required rather than simply yielding.
Students test whether fighting back and dying could count as honorable use of free will rather than forbidden suicide, but Jiang insists Dante would never simply say suicide is acceptable.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang states the medieval constraint as brutally as possible: suicide is worse than rape because the soul matters and the body does not.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the worst sin is suicide much more much worse than rape
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest theological pressure point and the premise that makes the free-will paradox so difficult.

signature_moments.moment: The whole moral calculus collapses into one contrast: the body belongs to earth, but the soul belongs to God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: your body belongs to this earth which is nothing but your soul belongs to god which is everything
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's most compressed restatement of why outward coercion should not settle the spiritual question.

signature_moments.moment: The class pushes right up to the taboo question of whether a death in resistance could be different from suicide, and Jiang refuses the easy escape hatch.
signature_moments.source_phrase: is dante saying that in this case suicide is okay... dante would never say suicide's okay
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's live edge: the classroom is probing for a loophole and Jiang will not allow the paradox to dissolve that quickly.

glossary_terms.term: body belongs to earth / soul belongs to God
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's compressed formula for the Christian ranking that treats bodily violation as secondary to the soul's fidelity to God.
A student's proposed category for resisting coercion to the point of death without calling it straightforward suicide.

chronology_notes.note: The discussion escalates from coerced vows to the harsher theological machinery behind them. Jiang now frames Piccarda's case through Augustine, suicide, and the body-soul split, then watches the class search for a form of resistance that would preserve both free will and orthodoxy.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's summary of Catholic teaching and Augustine is rhetorically compressed for classroom effect. Preserve it as his explanatory framing for Dante rather than as a full historical account of doctrine.
